title: TB9-12740
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellant appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), and requests that the RPD's decision be set aside and substituted with a determination that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Kenya, alleges that she is a lesbian and that she fears persecution based on her sexual orientation. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant lacked credibility and rejected her claim in a decision dated April 29, 2019.

The Appellant appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), and requests that the RPD's decision be set aside and substituted with a determination that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the matter be referred back to a different panel of the RPD for redetermination.1 DETERMINATION
The appeal is dismissed. I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.2 SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

The Appellant, a 25-year-old woman from Kenya, purportedly fears persecution as a lesbian. She was allegedly XXXX from XXXX in 2014 after kissing another female XXXX, which also resulted in threats from family members and the wider community. Most notably, an XXXX who claimed to be a member of the Mungiki gang assaulted the Appellant and her mother. The Appellant and her mother relocated to XXXX, another county in Nairobi, after neighbours began threatening to call the police.

The Appellant allegedly experienced additional incidents after she began dating a female XXXX in XXXX 2015. Police attended the XXXX and accused the Appellant and her partner of being in a "forbidden relationship," which they denied. Three men who claimed to be members of the Mungiki and associated with her uncle attacked the Appellant and her partner, and took their telephones and bags. The next day, the Appellant's uncle slapped and threatened her. The Appellant attempted to confide in her mother, but this resulted in an altercation and she was locked up in her room for the weekend. Her uncle attended her internship placement and caused a scene, which resulted in her dismissal.

The Appellant's uncle allegedly attempted to force her into an arrange marriage and kept her confined for two weeks in XXXX 2017. She managed to escape from her uncle's car while he was driving her to meet her future husband. Her same-sex partner arranged for her to stay at a cousin's home in XXXX. She eventually left XXXX to stay with a friend in XXXX after she received threatening text messages from her uncle and heard that a group of men were asking about her.

In XXXX 2017, a group of Mungiki members allegedly found the Appellant and her same-sex partner in XXXX and sexually assaulted them. The Appellant was taken to the hospital unconscious where she received treatment for two weeks. She did not hear from her same-sex partner again after the incident and believes that the Mungiki took her.

The Appellant relocated from XXXX to XXXX where she stayed with her mother's friend. Her mother also connected with an agent who helped the Appellant obtain a Canadian student visa to study at XXXX College. She left Kenya for Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018, and filed her claim for refugee protection on February 21, 2018. She claims that her mother and brother continue to face problems from her uncle since her departure from Kenya, and that her brother was taken in revenge but managed to escape.

The RPD found that the Appellant was not credible and did not establish her sexual orientation on a balance of probabilities because of omissions from her Basis of Claim form (BOC), inconsistencies in her evidence, and because she relied upon documents that are not genuine.

The Appellant did not submit new evidence with her appeal record, but subsequently provided evidence in response to a notice sent by the registrar of the RAD to all active appellants on June 15, 2020. The notice provided an opportunity to submit documents and a written submission within 30 days without an application because of the novel circumstances related to COVID-19. It notes that the admissibility requirements in section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), and Rule 29 would continue to apply.

The evidence includes statutory declarations from the Appellant and her mother with accompanying photographs, and two articles about the Mungiki and the overall effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on LGBTQ people throughout the world.

New evidence is only admissible before the RAD if it arose after the rejection of the claim, if it was not reasonably available, or if the Appellant could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time of the rejection of the claim.3 In addition to these legislative requirements, under the Federal Court of Appeal decisions in Singh and Raza, admissibility is limited to evidence that is relevant, new, and credible.4 Since these documents were not provided with the appeal record, they are also subject to Rule 29 of the RAD Rules which requires consideration of all relevant factors, including their relevance and probative value, any new evidence that they bring to the appeal, and whether they could have provided with the appeal record.

The documents meet the requirements for admissibility. The statutory declarations and photographs concern new incidents that allegedly occurred after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. The news articles postdate the claim and concern the re-emergence of the Mungiki in Kenya, and the increased vulnerability of LGBTQ people during the pandemic. Accordingly, these documents arose after the rejection of the claim, are new, and are relevant to the Appellant's claim. The articles were published by a major news outlet in Nairobi and a think tank from the United States which are credible sources. I see nothing on the face of the statutory declarations and photographs that raise concerns about their credibility. The new incidents recounted in these documents, the information they provide about the agents of harm, the current status of the Mungiki in Kenya, and the impact of COVID-19 on the existing inequalities and vulnerabilities of LGBTQ people, weigh in favour of their admissible under Rule 29. The documents are admitted and will be considered below.
The Appellant does not request an oral hearing before the RAD.
The determinative issue in this appeal is the Appellant's credibility.

The standard of correctness applies to this appeal as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.5 This requires an independent assessment of the refugee claim to determine whether the RPD was correct in its findings and determinations.6 While deference can be afforded to the RPD on specific issues when it enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, such an advantage does not arise in the present case.

After considering the Appellant's arguments and conducting an independent review of the entire record, including the transcript of the proceeding before the RPD, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant is not credible. As will be outlined below, the Appellant relied on fraudulent documents to establish central allegations to her claim, including that she was an active member of an organization that supports the LGBTQ community in Kenya, and that she was kidnapped in 2017 and hospitalized after a sexual assault. The Appellant also provided inconsistent evidence about who she informed about her sexual orientation in Kenya, and whether she ever attempted to obtain an affidavit from her current same-sex partner in Canada. These credibility findings go to the heart of her claim that she is a lesbian and that she experienced various incidents because of her sexual orientation, and therefore undermine her overall credibility. Reliance on fraudulent documents from an LGBTQ organization
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant's reliance on fraudulent documents to demonstrate her involvement in an organization supporting the LGBTQ community in Kenya undermines her credibility.

The Appellant provided a membership card and a letter from an LGBTQ organization in Kenya which is known by the acronym GALCK. The full name of the organization on the membership card and on both the letterhead and stamp of the supporting letter incorrectly refer to the name of the organization as the "Gays and Lesbians Community of Kenya." Evidence in the record from GALCK's website reveals that the proper name of the organization is the "Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya."

I agree with the RPD that the documents from GALCK are fraudulent because of the significant irregularities on their face. The Appellant could not provide an explanation for the irregularities at the hearing, and instead testified that she did not know why the full name of GALCK was different on her documents. The Appellant does not even address the RPD's findings concerning the documents from GALCK in her appeal memorandum.

The Appellant's alleged association with GALCK is an important part of her claim. According to her testimony, she was introduced to the organization by her same-sex partner, and the member of GALCK were among the very few people that she was able to open-up to about her sexual orientation. The letter from GALCK even states that the Appellant "had been an encouragement to many and those fearing to come out," and that "she made sure members in our organization felt accepted as the community".

Given the centrality of these documents to the Appellant's narrative about how her same-sex partner got her involved in the LGBTQ community in Kenya, how she opened up about her sexual orientation, and how she ultimately provided support and encouragement to other members of the LGBTQ community in Kenya, I agree with the RPD that her reliance on fraudulent documents from GALCK undermines her overall credibility. Reliance on fraudulent police report and medical documents

The Appellant also relied on fraudulent police and hospital records. The hospital reports and the police abstract/missing person reports the Appellant's mother and friend filed after she was allegedly kidnapped by her uncle contain irregular stamps that undermine the authenticity of these documents.

The RPD's observation that the stamps on these documents were meant to resemble a rubber wet stamp impression but yet were "pixelated, lacked any bleed through, and lacked the squash that would be associated with a wet seal stamp," correctly led it to conclude that these documents are not genuine.

I do not accept the argument that the documents could have been pre-stamped but still genuine. The stamps on these documents are on the signature line and are clearly meant to replicate rubber wet stamps which were placed on the documents when they were signed. As the Federal Court explained in Kamiak: "the Board was not in error in concluding that the seals should have been stamped, as opposed to ink jet printed, as the purpose of a seal is to prove the authenticity of a document."7

There is no merit to the argument that "the documents require forensic examination to prevent the member from becoming a witness in the proceeding by giving evidence." Contrary to this assertion, the Federal Court stated the following in Jacques: It is clear that the Board does not have an obligation to have documents reviewed by experts before concluding that they are fraudulent (Culinescu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 73). However, there must be some evidence before the Board on which to base a finding that a document is not genuine, unless the problem is apparent on the document's face (Kashif v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FCT 179; Riveros v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 1009).8 Given the irregularities with the stamps on the face of the police and hospital reports, there is no merit to the argument that the RPD's reliance on the Federal Court decision in Jacques is misplaced. The Appellant points out that the documents in Kamiak were forensically examined, although I see nothing in the caselaw that requires forensic examination when a problem is apparent on the face of the document.

These fraudulent documents undermine the Appellant's credibility because she relied on them to establish some of the most significant incidents in her claim, including the allegation that she was kidnapped by her uncle to be forced her into an arranged marriage, and that she was sexually assaulted by members of the Mungiki gang. Who did the Appellant inform about her sexual orientation?
Inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence about who she informed about her sexual orientation in Kenya also undermine her credibility.

The Appellant's testimony that she only spoke about her sexual orientation with her partner, her mother, her uncle, and the "Gays and Lesbians Community of Kenya," is inconsistent with the information in the BOC, in which she indicates that she also informed her friend and her partner's cousin in addition to these people.

I do not accept the argument that this "at best this tests her memory, not her sexuality." The Appellant did not actually attribute the inconsistency to her memory when the inconsistency was raised by the RPD at the hearing, but instead merely acknowledged that she had told her friend and her partner's cousin when she was given an opportunity to provide an explanation. The Appellant amended the BOC on March 15, 2019, to include her friend and her partner's cousin as people she informed about her sexual orientation. This amendment made the BOC uniform with the affidavits from these two people as they indicate that the Appellant opened-up to them. Since the amendment was made only ten days prior to the hearing, the suggestion that the inconsistency may be a result of a lapse in memory without further elaboration is not a reasonable explanation.

Nor do I accept the submission that "it is understandable that a list of people she told she is a lesbian is not foremost in her mind," because of the "severe nature of the harm she faced." Contrary to the argument, the severe homophobic incidents which the Appellant alleges to have experienced in Kenya is the very reason why she would have remained more diligent about who she informed about her sexual orientation. I therefore agree with the RPD that the inconsistencies about who the Appellant informed about her sexual orientation undermine her overall credibility. Inconsistencies about current same-sex partner
The RPD correctly drew an adverse inference from inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence on whether she attempted to obtain a letter or affidavit from her current same-sex partner in Canada.

The Appellant testified that she was in a same-sex relationship in Canada but was unsuccessful at obtaining a supporting letter or affidavit from her partner. This was inconsistent with her earlier testimony that the only document she was unsuccessful at obtaining was an affidavit from her previous partner's mother in Kenya.

While the Appellant submits that she believed that the RPD was referring to evidence from Kenya, I do not accept this as a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. The RPD did not limit its question solely to documents from Kenya, but rather asked the Appellant more broadly, "are there any documents out there that you took steps to get but you could not actually get it." After she testified about her inability to obtain an affidavit from the mother of her former partner in Kenya, the RPD asked whether there were "any other documents," to which she answered "no."

The RPD also gave the Appellant an opportunity to submit copies of alleged text messages with her same-sex partner in Canada which she referred to in testimony as corroborative evidence of her relationship to help resolve the inconsistency. This was because the Appellant testified that she possessed text messages in which her same-sex partner inquired whether "I want to meet up and have sex?" Given the credibility concerns surrounding the Appellant's attempt at obtaining a letter or affidavit from her same-sex partner, the RPD was correct to give the Appellant this opportunity to provide corroborative evidence. This meets the two-step analysis for considering the availability of corroborative evidence as outlined in the Federal Court's decision in Horvath and recently reiterated in Senadheerage: Corroborative evidence was only required if the RAD had (1) reason to doubt the Applicants' claim and (2) the corroborating evidence could reasonably be expected to be available [...].9 The Appellant did not subsequently submit any of the text messages, despite the suggestion that copies could be submitted after the hearing but before the RPD renders its decision.

The Appellant's current same-sex relationship in Canada goes to the heart of her claim that she is lesbian and that she fears persecution in Kenya based on her sexual orientation. I thus agree with the RDP that her conflicting testimony on whether she attempted to obtain a letter or affidavit from her same-sex partner undermines her credibility. The concern is not with the lack of corroborating evidence, but rather her conflicting testimony on whether she ever attempted to obtain a letter or affidavit. I therefore do not accept the argument that "the RPD was not entitled to hold against the Appellant that she was unable to get an affidavit from her girlfriend in Canada and she failed to mention that at the outset of the hearing when asked whether there was any evidence she was unable to obtain."

While the RPD made additional adverse inferences based on inconsistencies in the evidence and omissions from the BOC, I do not need to address those findings since I find that the credibility concerns outlined above, for which the Appellant did not provide reasonable explanations, fully rebut the presumption of truthfulness.10 These credibility findings concern the Appellant's alleged sexual orientation and incidents that are central to her claim, and therefore undermine her overall credibility.

In reaching this determination, I remained mindful of both the challenges experienced by some people when presenting evidence about their sexual orientation, and the need to avoid stereotyping and inappropriate assumptions about diverse sexual minorities as outlined in the Chairperson's Guideline: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE). The RPD's credibility findings were not based on stereotypes or assumptions, but rather on inconsistencies in the Appellant's own evidence and her reliance on fraudulent documents. The Appellant did not provide reasonable explanations in which the inconsistencies can be attributed to cultural, psychological, or other barriers as outlined in the SOGIE Guideline. The Documentary Evidence

The balance of the documentary evidence in the record does not resolve the credibility concerns outlined above or independently establish the Appellant's sexual orientation. Credibility findings based on inconsistencies are dispositive of a claim unless they are resolved by the documentary evidence.11

The Appellant's counsel argues that "it would be nonsensical for the Appellant to disclose the photographs to prove a mere friendship," although photographs of the Appellant posing with other women do not help resolve the credibility concerns outlined above or establish her sexual orientation.

A letter confirming the Appellant's involvement with the XXXX XXXX does not establish her sexual orientation as a lesbian in light of credibility concerns outlined above. Since the Appellant testified that she met her same-sex partner in Canada at the XXXX, without some resolution to the inconsistencies in her evidence about this partner a letter from the XXXX which indicates that she attended an orientation session and participated in some LGBTQ programs does not on its own establish her sexual orientation on a balance of probabilities.

While the Appellant points out that the RPD failed to refer to a letter from her former XXXX in Kenya which indicates that she was XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, because she is a lesbian, I am not satisfied that the letter is a credible source of information because of inconsistencies in the evidence. The letter indicates that she was being XXXX because of "public indecency and Lesbianism," after she was given "several warnings and speaking to your XXXX." Contrary to this account, the Appellant testified that she was never given a warning and was instead immediately XXXX. The Appellant's explanation that the XXXX "exaggerated" is not a reasonable explanation since the concern is not with the description of the incident but rather the question of whether she was XXXX immediately or after receiving several warnings. This inconsistency undermines the credibility of this document and I accordingly place no weight on it.

I do not accept the argument that the "four people swore affidavits that corrobrate essential elements of the refugee claim." All four affidavits refer to the Appellant as being a lesbian in the context of the incidents from 2014 and 2017. Without resolution to the credibility concerns related to those incidents as outlined above, I am not satisifed that the mere reference to the Appellant as being as a lesbian in those affidavits is sufficient to establish her sexual orientation on a balance of probabilities.

Lastly, the new evidence submitted by the Appellant does not resolve the credibility concerns outlined above or independently establish her sexual orientation as a lesbian, on a balance of probabilities. Her mother recounts three incidents that were alleged perpetrated against her by the uncle and the Mungiki gang, as well as photographs of property damage. The Appellant's mother does not, however, indicate that the perpetrators of those incidents told her that they were motivated by the Appellant's sexual orientation, and instead merely states that "they demanded that I produce my 'cursed' daughter." She also states that she "believe[s] that the police failed to pursue justice due to my daughter's sexual orientation." While the Appellant states in her affidavit that she attended the XXXX XXXX and a XXXX event in 2019, and fears that her increase screening at the airport due to Covid-19 may result in her sexual orientation being revealed, none of this resolves the credibility concerns or otherwise establishes her sexual orientation, on a balance of probabilities. Accordingly, the news articles on the resurgence of the Munkiki gang and the effects of the pandemic on LGBTQ people throughout the world do not establish the Appellant's sexual orientation.

Lastly, since I find that the Appellant is not credible regarding her sexual orientation, I do not need to assess whether she faces a serious possibility of persecution based on the overall treatment of sexual minorities in Kenya.

For the reasons outlined above, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant was not credible and has not established her sexual orientation as a lesbian on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant therefore does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Kenya, nor, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Kenya.

The decision of the RPD is confirmed and the appeal is dismissed.12 John Helis John Helis December 10, 2020 Date 1 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 111(1)(b) & 111(1)(c) [IRPA]. 2 IRPA s. 111(1)(a). 3 IRPA s. 110(4). 4 Raza v.
